'''Beauprez''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Bill Owens (Colorado politician)|Bill Owens]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Bill Ritter]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsCO}} The '''2006 Colorado gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Republican governor [[Bill Owens (Colorado politician)|Bill Owens]] was unable to run due to term limits, and the election was won by Democratic nominee [[Bill Ritter]]. With his win, Democrats obtained a trifecta in the state for the first time since 1963. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time the Governor's office in Colorado changed partisan control. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Bill Ritter]], former [[Denver District Attorney's Office|District Attorney of Denver]] ===Campaign=== In the leadup to the Democratic primary, [[Bill Ritter]], the former [[Denver District Attorney's Office|District Attorney of Denver]], emerged as the leading Democratic candidate. Though several other prominent state Democrats, including Denver Mayor [[John Hickenlooper]]{{cite news|date=February 6, 2006|title=Hickenlooper Won't Run for Governor|work=Summit Daily News|location=[[Breckenridge, Colorado]]|url=https://www.summitdaily.com/news/hickenlooper-wont-run-for-governor/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} and State House Speaker [[Andrew Romanoff]],{{cite news|date=January 4, 2006|title=Romanoff Passes on Governor's Race|work=Denver Business Journal|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/denver/stories/2006/01/02/daily16.html|access-date=July 5, 2022}} considered running for Governor, both ultimately declined to do so. State Representative Gary Lindstrom, the only other candidate besides Ritter in the race, ended his campaign on February 28, 2006.{{cite news|date=February 28, 2006|title=Lindstrom Drops out of Governor's Race|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/02/28/lindstrom-drops-out-of-governors-race-2/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} Ritter's personal opposition to abortion motivated pro-choice leaders in the state party to seek alternatives to him,{{cite news|date=April 15, 2006|title=Democrat Sidesteps the Abortion Plank|last=Riccardi|first=Nicholas|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|location=[[Los Angeles, California]]|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2006-apr-15-na-governor15-story.html|access-date=July 5, 2022}} but none ultimately materialized, and opposition to Ritter softened with his pledge to not alter the state's liberal abortion laws.{{cite news|date=February 14, 2006|title=Ritter Walks percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Bob Beauprez]], U.S. Congressman from [[Colorado's 7th congressional district]] ===Campaign=== With popular two-term Governor [[Bill Owens (Colorado politician)|Bill Owens]] barred from seeking re-election, an open race developed for the Republican nomination to succeed him. The race looked like it would be between Congressman [[Bob Beauprez]], who represented the swingy Denver suburbs in Congress, and former [[University of Denver]] President [[Marc Holtzman]]. The race between Beauprez and Holtzman was contentious. Beauprez accused Holtzman of ethics violations, including making false allegations that the campaign's email list was stolen,{{cite news|date=June 22, 2006|title=Holtzman's Run is Done|last=Crummy|first=Karen|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/06/22/holtzmans-run-is-done/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} providing falsified poll results to the ''[[Denver Post]]'', and using a separate state campaign committee as a "shadow gubernatorial campaign."{{cite news|date=May 1, 2006|title=Holtzman Calls Outside Probe Unnecessary|last=Crummy|first=Karen|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/05/01/holtzman-calls-outside-probe-unnecessary/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} Holtzman, meanwhile, accused Beauprez of being part of the "politics of power" that he argued had taken the party away from its conservative values, pointing to Beauprez's support of Referendum C in 2005, which allowed the state to hold onto excess tax revenues rather than refund surpluses.{{cite news|date=January 6, 2006|title=Holtzman to GOP: 'Take Back the Party'|last=Roper|first=Peter|work=[[Pueblo Chieftain]]|location=[[Pueblo, Colorado]]|url=https://www.chieftain.com/story/news/2006/01/07/holtzman-to-gop-take-back/8432644007/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} In the end, the campaign between the two frontrunners fizzled. Beauprez won a landslide victory at the state Republican convention, denying Holtzman a spot on the ballot. Holtzman's efforts to collect signatures to win a spot on the ballot were ultimately in vain, with the [[Colorado Supreme Court]] ruling in June that he had failed to submit enough signatures. In response, Holtzman suspended his campaign and endorsed Beauprez, who won the Republican primary unopposed. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Bob Beauprez | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 193,804 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 193,804 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Campaign== === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- !
